_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season10-bible-v1.0.1.md row a10e08, writer brief a10e08-v1.0.0.md, LATENT catalog v1.0.79 and latent-syllabus-v1.0.3.md. a10e07's next field (only that field was read) was honoured: a motorway's overnight resurfacing crews, and the programs that serve a model compared in plain words: vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. Keeps apart from a6e09 (there the model changed; here the engine changes and the model stays), from s9e13, s9e07 and s9e18 (the lane closure is only the 22:00 start: no animals, buses or parking), from s9e16 (one contrast line: there a batch waited to fill; here the engine could not hold more), from the retired garage setting (no garage or cars) and from a10e01's furnace (no hot asphalt plant shown). Shared given data: Llama 3.1 8B, 16.06 billion bytes in 16 bits, about 15 GB on the card's meter, 128 KB of working memory a token; one H100, 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s; sizes in the meter's units (1 GB = 1,024 MB), speeds in the maker's. Story data: each question carries its crew's method statement, about 1,500 tokens, and each summary is 500 tokens, so 250 MB of working memory an answer; the card at $4.29 an hour, Lambda's list price for a single H100 SXM read 16 October 2026; a month 730 hours. Ulceby's own measurements, never a source's: vLLM 45 tokens a second each with 64 at once (first word 0.3 s) and 55 with up to 16 (0.2 s); TensorRT-LLM 72 with up to 16 (0.2 s), and, built for 64, 54 with 64 at once (0.3 s, Aurelijus's replay on Thursday 8 October). The published benchmark is only named, never given numbers. Story arithmetic (all in sims/a10e08-v1.0.0.js): 500 / 72 = 6.9 s; waves at 0, 6.9, 13.9 and 20.8 s; first words 0.2, 7.1, 14.1 and 21.0 s; last answer 27.8 s; 500 / 45 = 11.1 s; 500 / 55 = 9.1 s; 72 / 55 = 1.31, the dashboard's 30%; two copies 32 slots, 2 waves, 7.1 s and 13.9 s, $6,263 against $3,132 a month; built for 64 one wave, 9.3 s, memory 15 GB + 64 x 250 MB = 30.6 GB of 80; 16 a minute from 22:00, every first word 0.2 s, last answer 22:03:06.9. Timeline: last week's peak Wednesday 30 September 2026; benchmark read the week before the switch; engine built on the morning of Wednesday 7 October, tested at 13:00 with 12 at once, switched at 14:00; first 22:00 start that night; the radio from 22:00:12; the post at about 06:00 on Thursday 8 October; closures again at 22:00 that night. One deliberate change from the brief: the alert is the radio filling from 22:00:12, still busy at 22:01, because every answer had arrived by 22:00:27.8. Cold case: 2 months later, 8 October to Monday 7 December 2026 (the build for 64 live from Thursday 8 October; the second contract won Monday 2 November; its 16 crews joined from Monday 7 December): 80 at 22:00, 64 run at 54 a second (9.3 s), 16 wait, second-wave first word 9.5 s, last answer 16.2 s; memory for 80: 34.5 GB of 80. Standards note conditional, not legal advice. Sources read 16 October 2026.
title: The Engines

post.author: u/night_gang_ebele
post.title: I supervise a motorway's night resurfacing crews. Our dashboard says the assistant answers 30% faster than last week. Last night 16 crews waited 21 seconds for its first word.

blocks.text: I'm Ebele, night gang supervisor for Ulceby Highways. We resurface the motorway past Hatherop, in lanes closed by permits from 22:00.
Our 64 crew leaders each get a method statement: their job's steps and safety rules.
Our assistant sums it up in about 500 tokens, the small pieces of text a language model writes.
It's Llama 3.1 8B. Its weights, its learned numbers, take 16.06 billion bytes, about 15 GB, on one rented graphics card: an NVIDIA H100 with 80 GB.

Between card and tablets sits the program that loads the model, takes questions and returns answers: a serving engine. One recipe, kitchens laid out differently: same dish, different pace. Until yesterday ours was vLLM.
An engine writes many answers side by side, one token each at a time. Engineers call the group a batch, and each answer's place a slot.
Each answer keeps working memory on the card, 128 KB, about 131,000 bytes, a token. vLLM hands it out a page at a time and lets in as many answers as free memory holds.
On Wednesday 30 September, at our 22:00 peak, the night's busiest minute, vLLM ran all 64 answers at once: first word in 0.3 s, 45 tokens a second each, done in 11.1 s.

Last week Aurelijus in IT read a published benchmark: TensorRT-LLM, NVIDIA's engine, faster on the H100. A benchmark is a replay: record questions with their arrival times and lengths, play them into each engine at the same times, compare.

TensorRT-LLM is built before it runs: choose the model and card, fix the largest batch it may run, a build-time limit, then compile it into a program for that card. Yesterday, Wednesday 7 October, Aurelijus built ours from the benchmark's recipe.

At 13:00 he tested both with 12 questions at once: TensorRT-LLM 72 tokens a second each, 6.9 s an answer; vLLM 55 tokens a second. At 14:00 he switched, and typed on the assistant's dashboard of timings: "answers 30% faster than last week".
Last night was its first 22:00. From 22:00:12 the radio filled: is the assistant down? By 22:01 every answer had arrived; the calls kept coming.
Each line: the time, then what the engine did.

22:00:00.0  64 questions arrive. 16 answers start, 48 questions wait.
22:00:06.9  16 answers finish. 16 more answers start, 32 questions wait.
22:00:13.9  16 answers finish. 16 more answers start, 16 questions wait.
22:00:20.8  16 answers finish. the last 16 answers start.
22:00:21.0  the last 16 crews get their first word.
22:00:27.8  the last 16 answers finish.
Tjarda's crew stood in their coned lane, planer idling, tablet blank for 21 seconds, while the card we rent by the hour wrote 16 answers with room for 64 answers.

The last 16 crews saw a first word at 21.0 s and the last answer ended at 27.8 s. The bottom row is the week before on vLLM: all 64 answers at once, done in 11.1 s.

blocks.text: By hand: 500 tokens ÷ 72 tokens a second = 6.9 s an answer. The recipe's largest batch was 16 answers: 16 run, 48 questions wait, and as each wave ends the next 16 start. The last answer ends at 4 waves × 6.94 s = 27.8 s.
The dashboard's 30% is 72 ÷ 55 tokens a second = 1.31 times, from 12 answers at once. The limit was 16 answers.
Aurelijus says the benchmark is public and 72 beats 55 tokens a second: spread the crews out. Closures start at 22:00 tonight. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing on the motorway is haunted, though a blank tablet in a coned lane at night would chill anyone. The wait for an answer's first word has a name: time to first token, TTFT for short (a10e02). There is a third engine you didn't try, SGLang, which keeps the working memory of question beginnings that many questions share and reuses it. Two questions. How many answers ran at once in yesterday's test, and how many at 22:00? And where is the largest batch written down, and when was it set?

replies.author: u/night_gang_ebele
replies.text: 12 answers in the test; 64 answers at 22:00. The 16 is in the build settings Aurelijus copied from the benchmark's recipe, set yesterday morning when he built the engine. Each crew's method statement is its own job's, so our questions share only a few opening words.

comments.author: u/it_lead_aurelijus
comments.text: I read that benchmark end to end. It's public, it's on the maker's own card, and 72 beats 55 tokens a second. We don't need to record a night of our own and play it back into each engine; the benchmark already did that. The engine is fine. Our crews all tap in the same second, so tune the crews, not the engine: ask them to send their questions a few minutes apart.

replies.author: u/night_gang_ebele
replies.text: How many questions at once did the benchmark's recipe allow?

replies.author: u/it_lead_aurelijus
replies.text: 16 answers. Whoever published it knows that engine better than we do.

comments.author: u/contracts_manager_mehmood
comments.text: The new engine is faster per answer; it just needs more room. Rent a second H100 and run a second copy of the same engine on it: an identical engine on its own card, with the questions shared between the two. Twice the slots for $4.29 an hour more. That's cheaper than one crew standing idle.

comments.author: u/crew_leader_tjarda
comments.text: I don't mind which engine. Last night my crew stood in a live closure with the planer idling and a blank tablet. The permit says 22:00, and the summary tells me what changed in tonight's job since last night. The week before it came in about 11 seconds. Whatever you pick has to answer when the permit goes live.

replies.author: u/night_gang_ebele
replies.text: That was vLLM: all 64 answers at once, every one done in 11.1 s.

reply.prompt: It's 06:00 on Thursday 8 October, and the closures start at 22:00 tonight. What should Ulceby change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Run a second copy of the new engine on another card to double the slots.
options.part2: On Thursday Mehmood rented a second H100 at $4.29 an hour and Aurelijus ran a second copy of the 16-slot build on it, the questions shared between the two: 32 slots for 64 crews. At 22:00 each card ran 16 answers and kept 16 waiting. The second wave's first words came at 7.1 s and the last answer at 13.9 s: half of Wednesday's 27.8 s, and still later than vLLM's 11.1 s the week before. Tjarda's crew was in a second wave and waited 7.1 s with the planer idling. The card bill rose from $3,132 to $6,263 a month.
options.senior: A second copy doubles the slots, not the thinking behind them. Each copy still runs at most 16 answers and queues the rest, so 64 questions make two waves instead of four. You pay for a second card to work around a number typed in at build time, and the moment the crews pass 32 the waves come back. Measure the peak first, size the build to it, and add cards only when the peak needs more than one card can hold.

options.text: Replay our own 22:00 peak on each engine, and build its limits from it.
options.part2: On Thursday morning Aurelijus took Wednesday's 22:00 from the log: 64 questions at 22:00:00.0, each with its method statement's length and its summary's. He played it, at the same times, into vLLM, into the engine as built, and into a new build with a largest batch of 64, after checking the memory: 15 GB of weights plus 64 × 250 MB of working memory, 30.6 GB of the card's 80. vLLM finished at 11.1 s, the 16-slot build at 27.8 s in four waves, and the build for 64 in one wave: first word in 0.3 s, 54 tokens a second each, every answer done in 9.3 s. At 22:00 on Thursday the build for 64 ran every crew at once; Tjarda's tablet showed its first word in 0.3 s, and the radio stayed quiet. The dashboard's 30% came down; it now shows each night's longest wait for a first word.
options.senior: A benchmark measures someone else's traffic with someone else's settings. Before switching engines, record your own busiest minute, the arrival times and the lengths, play it into each engine exactly as it will run, and compare what your people feel: the first word and the last answer, not one tokens-a-second figure. Then set every limit fixed at build time from that peak, check the memory it needs, and leave room to grow. The afternoon test had 12 answers and the limit was 16: a test below a limit can never find it.

options.text: Go back to the old engine, which sizes its batch from free memory.
options.verdict: Safe at night, slower by day
options.part2: On Thursday Aurelijus switched back to vLLM. At 22:00 it ran all 64 answers at once, as the week before: first word in 0.3 s, 45 tokens a second each, every answer done in 11.1 s. Nobody radioed, and Tjarda's crew had its summary before the planer warmed up. By day, with about 12 questions at once, answers took 9.1 s instead of the new engine's 6.9 s, 55 tokens a second against 72, and Aurelijus took the 30% off the dashboard. Nobody measured the new engine at the peak, so which engine serves Ulceby best stayed an open question.
options.senior: An honest retreat. vLLM decides how many answers run together from free memory as it runs, so all 64 fit, and there is nothing to rebuild for each model and card. The price is speed at the afternoon load: 55 tokens a second against 72, close to a quarter slower. It also leaves the lesson unlearned: the engine was switched on a benchmark and on a test below the night's peak, and the next switch will be made the same way unless someone replays the peak first.

options.text: Ask crew leaders to send their questions a few minutes apart at 22:00.
options.part2: On Thursday Ebele radioed a rota: crews 1 to 16 at 22:00, 17 to 32 at 22:01, 33 to 48 at 22:02, 49 to 64 at 22:03. Each group that kept to it had a first word in 0.2 s and a summary in 6.9 s; the last group's answers ended at 22:03:06.9. But every closure's permit starts at 22:00, and crews do not stand still in a live closure. Two leaders in the last group set out from the night before's summary. Tonight's method statement for one of them had marked a gully, a drain inlet in the road, in the strip their planer was due to cut. Ebele caught it on the radio at 22:20, before the planer reached it.
options.senior: Spreading the questions treats the engine's limit as the crews' problem. The 22:00 start is set by the closure permits, not by the crews, so the work either waits or starts without its briefing, and every crew added to the night makes the rota longer. A queue that forms because of a number fixed at build time is fixed in the build, measured against the real peak.

sim.title: Replay 22:00 on Ulceby's assistant
sim.lede: You're Ebele at 21:59 on Wednesday 7 October 2026, a minute before the first 22:00 start on the new engine. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: Llama 3.1 8B, 16.06 billion bytes of weights in 16 bits, about 15 GB on the card's meter (1 GB = 1,024 MB), and 128 KB of working memory per token; one rented H100 with 80 GB, reading its memory at 3.35 TB a second (the maker's 1,000), at $4.29 an hour; a month is 730 hours. Each question carries its crew's method statement, about 1,500 tokens, and every summary is 500 tokens: 2,000 tokens × 128 KB = 250 MB of working memory an answer. Ulceby's own measurements, never a source's: vLLM writes 45 tokens a second each with 64 answers at once, first word in 0.3 s, and 55 with up to 16 at once, first word in 0.2 s; TensorRT-LLM writes 72 with up to 16 at once, first word in 0.2 s (the afternoon test at 12, and each wave of 16 in Wednesday night's log), and, built for 64, 54 with 64 at once, first word in 0.3 s (Aurelijus's replay on Thursday). Other loads on one card were not measured, and the sim says so. vLLM lets in answers as free memory allows; TensorRT-LLM runs at most the largest batch fixed when it was built, and the rest wait for a free slot.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the opening view is the afternoon test, 12 at once on the build for 16: 0.2 s to the first word, 6.9 s an answer. Play 22:00 and watch four waves: first words at 0.2, 7.1, 14.1 and 21.0 s, the last answer at 27.8 s. Switch to vLLM: one wave, 11.1 s; then set 12 questions and compare 9.1 s with 6.9 s. Back on the build for 16 at 64, try 2 copies, then 16 a minute. Build for 64. Then play each reply, and last, set 80 questions on the build for 64 for the cold case.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the motorway was haunted. TensorRT-LLM was built from a benchmark's recipe with a largest batch of 16 answers, a limit fixed at build time. The afternoon test ran 12, under it, so it passed at 72 tokens a second. At 22:00, 64 crews asked at once: 16 answers ran and 48 waited, and four waves of 6.9 s put the last first words at 21.0 s and the last answer at 27.8 s.

steps.title: What a serving engine does, and how the three differ.
steps.text: First, the engine loads the model's weights onto the card, 16.06 billion bytes here. Second, it takes questions as they arrive and gives each a slot in the batch. Third, in each step it reads the weights once and gives every answer in the batch one more token; on an H100 at 3.35 TB a second that read alone takes at least 4.8 ms. Fourth, it returns finished answers and fills their slots from the queue (continuous batching, a10e04). vLLM does this with working memory handed out a page at a time (PagedAttention, a10e03), sizes its batch from free memory as it runs, and supports many models and kinds of card. SGLang adds reuse of shared beginnings: it keeps the working memory of prompts' opening tokens in a tree and reuses it (RadixAttention), and a cache-aware router in front of several copies sends a question to the copy most likely to hold its beginning. TensorRT-LLM, NVIDIA's engine, batches in flight with paged memory too, but is built before it runs, with its limits fixed in the build. What can go wrong: choosing among them on a speed someone else measured on their own traffic.

steps.title: Building an engine, and the limit the build fixes.
steps.text: First, choose the model and the card. Second, fix the limits, among them the largest batch: the most answers it will ever run at once. Third, compile: turn the model and those settings into a program for that card. TensorRT-LLM's tuning page says the max batch size is set in the build config, or passed as --max_batch_size to trtllm-build, and its own sweep compared 64, 512 and the default 2048. The benchmark's recipe set 16, and Aurelijus copied it with the speed. NVIDIA's TensorRT page adds that, by default, a TensorRT engine is tied to the TensorRT version and the GPU it was built on, so a new card means a new build. What can go wrong: copying a recipe's limits along with its speed, because they were chosen for someone else's traffic.

steps.title: Waves: 16 run, the rest wait.
steps.text: First, 64 questions arrive at 22:00:00.0. Second, 16 take the 16 slots and 48 wait in the queue, though the card had room: 16 answers' working memory is 16 × 250 MB = 3.9 GB beside 15 GB of weights on an 80 GB card. Third, every summary is 500 tokens, so at 72 tokens a second each the 16 end together, 500 ÷ 72 = 6.9 s later. Fourth, the next 16 take the free slots. Waves start at 0, 6.9, 13.9 and 20.8 s; first words reach the four groups at 0.2, 7.1, 14.1 and 21.0 s; the last answer ends at 27.8 s. The tuning page draws the same thing small: a request that cannot be scheduled, even though there is space for it, because of the max batch size. vLLM, sizing its batch from free memory, ran all 64 at 45 tokens a second each: 11.1 s. Dead Letter's s9e16 held a batch open to fill it; here the engine never waited to fill a batch, it could not hold more. What can go wrong: a build-time limit gives no warning; it shows only as a queue.

steps.title: Why the test passed, and what a replay would have caught.
steps.text: The afternoon test ran 12 answers at once, under the limit of 16, so nothing waited: 72 tokens a second against vLLM's 55, and 72 ÷ 55 = 1.31, the dashboard's 30%. The dashboard compared two afternoon figures and called it last week. A replay does it with your own night: first, record the peak, the 64 arrivals at 22:00:00 with each question's and summary's length; second, play them into each engine as built, at the same times; third, compare the first word and the last answer each crew would see. It would have shown four waves before the switch. Ulceby's replay of a build for 64, after a memory check (15 GB + 64 × 250 MB = 30.6 GB of 80), gave one wave: first word in 0.3 s, 54 tokens a second each, 9.3 s. This is a6e09's re-test before switching, with the engine as the change and the model kept. What can go wrong: a re-test below the limit, which can never meet it.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fall short.
steps.text: Two copies of the 16-slot build give 32 slots: two waves, first words by 7.1 s and the last answer at 13.9 s, for $6,263 a month instead of $3,132, and waves again once crews pass 32. Sending the questions 16 a minute gives 0.2 s first words, but the last group's answers end at 22:03:06.9, and the permits start every closure at 22:00, so crews start without their summaries. Going back to vLLM brings back 11.1 s at the peak with nothing to rebuild, but 9.1 s against 6.9 s at the afternoon's 12. A longer timeout in the app changes nothing: the last crews still wait 21.0 s. What can go wrong: fixing the crews or the bill instead of the build.

diagram.aria: Wednesday's 22:00 replayed on four set-ups, and the replay's three steps. Top row: built for 16, 4 waves, last answer 27.8 seconds; two copies of 16, 2 waves on 2 cards, 13.9 seconds at $6,263 a month; vLLM, 1 wave at 45 tokens a second each, 11.1 seconds; built for 64, 1 wave at 54 each, 9.3 seconds. Bottom row: record the peak, 64 questions at 22:00:00 with their lengths; play them into each engine as built at the same times; compare the first word and the last answer, then set the limits. Note: memory for 64 is 15 GB plus 64 times 250 MB, 30.6 GB of 80.

notes.text: Memory for 64: 15 GB + 64 x 250 MB = 30.6 GB of 80

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: the same 64 questions on four set-ups. The build for 16 makes four waves; a second copy halves them at twice the bill; vLLM runs them all at once at 45 tokens a second each; the build for 64 runs them all at once at 54. fix.title: The fix: replay our own 22:00 peak on each engine and build the limits from it
fix.text: Record the real peak: Wednesday's 64 arrivals at 22:00:00, each with its question's and summary's length. Play it, at the same times, into each candidate engine exactly as built: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM as built for 16, and a new build with a largest batch of at least 64 after a memory check (15 GB + 64 × 250 MB = 30.6 GB of 80). Compare the first word and the last answer each crew would see. Here the build for 64 wins: one wave, 0.3 s to the first word, 9.3 s an answer. Replace the dashboard's typed 30% with each night's longest wait for a first word and how many questions waited for a slot, and run the replay again before any change to the engine, the model, the card or the number of crews.

limits: A replay is only as good as the night it recorded. When the crews or the method statements grow, the peak changes, and the replay and the build must be redone (the cold case). Leave headroom, and watch the longest wait for a first word every night.

The speeds here, 45, 55, 72 and 54 tokens a second, are Ulceby's own measurements on its card and its questions, not a source's, and engines change month to month: re-measure after any upgrade of the engine, the model or the card.

TensorRT-LLM's tuning page names a second build-time limit, max num tokens, and advises trying combinations of both; a replay should sweep them. Newer versions may also offer other ways to set limits: check the page for the version you run.

explain.seniorTake: A serving engine is the kitchen around the recipe: the model stays the same, and the engine decides how many answers cook at once, where their working memory goes and who waits. vLLM sizes its batch from free memory as it runs, with paged memory and continuous batching, across many models and cards. SGLang adds reuse of shared prompt beginnings and a router that sends a question to the copy most likely to hold its beginning. TensorRT-LLM, NVIDIA's engine, is built for its model and card with limits fixed in the build, and can be the fastest of the three below those limits. A benchmark tells you how an engine ran someone else's traffic with someone else's settings; it cannot tell you about a limit your peak will meet. So before any switch, replay your own busiest minute into each engine exactly as it will run, compare the first word and the last answer your people would feel, set every build-time limit from that peak with the memory checked, and keep the dashboard on live waits, not a typed percentage. Behind one front door (a6e01) users never see which kitchen cooked their answer; they only feel the wait.

realWorld.title: TensorRT-LLM: the largest batch is set at build
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's "Tuning Max Batch Size and Max Num Tokens" page says "You can specify the max batch size in the build config." and, for the command-line flow, "pass `--max_batch_size <int>` to `trtllm-build` to tune max batch size." Its own sweep compared "max batch sizes of 64, 512, and the default 2048". Ulceby's 16 came from a recipe, not the default.

realWorld.title: TensorRT-LLM: room to spare, and still waiting
realWorld.text: In the same page's small example, with a max batch size of 4: "It cannot schedule the last request, Request 5, even though there is space for it in the max num tokens budget" "because of the max batch size limit of 4." It advises: "It is important to set the max batch size large enough that it doesn’t bottleneck the scheduling of new requests."

realWorld.title: TensorRT-LLM: in-flight batching and paged memory
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's overview says "TensorRT LLM is NVIDIA’s comprehensive open-source library for accelerating and optimizing inference performance" "of the latest large language models (LLMs) on NVIDIA GPUs." It lists "In-flight batching eliminates wait times by dynamically managing request execution," and "Paged KV cache with intelligent block reuse and memory optimization".

realWorld.title: TensorRT: an engine for one GPU
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's TensorRT capabilities page says "By default, TensorRT engines are specific to both the TensorRT version and the GPU on which they were created." That is the base library's page; for a TensorRT-LLM build, check the version you run.

realWorld.title: vLLM: paged memory, continuous batching, many cards
realWorld.text: vLLM's documentation home says "vLLM is a fast and easy-to-use library for LLM inference and serving." Among its features: "Efficient management of attention key and value memory with PagedAttention", "Continuous batching of incoming requests, chunked prefill, prefix caching" and "Support for NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and x86/ARM/PowerPC CPUs."

realWorld.title: SGLang: reusing shared beginnings
realWorld.text: SGLang's documentation home calls it a "High-performance serving framework for large language and multimodal models." "Designed for low-latency, high-throughput inference with RadixAttention, prefix caching, and multi-GPU parallelism." Ulceby's questions share only a few opening words, so this strength would help them little.

realWorld.title: SGLang's paper: RadixAttention
realWorld.text: Zheng and colleagues' paper, "SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs", says "The runtime accelerates execution with novel optimizations like RadixAttention for KV cache reuse" and "Experiments show that SGLang achieves up to 6.4x higher throughput compared to state-of-the-art inference systems", on their tests, not Ulceby's.

realWorld.title: SGLang v0.4: a router that follows the cache
realWorld.text: LMSYS's post of 4 December 2024 says "The load balancer predicts prefix KV cache hit rates on workers and selects those with the highest match rates." and "Requests are sent to workers with a higher hit rate, and load balancing is performed to avoid imbalance." It reports "up to 1.9x increase in throughput with 3.8x higher cache hit rate" on their benchmark.

realWorld.title: H100: 80 GB and the memory road
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's H100 page gives the H100 SXM 80GB of GPU memory and a GPU memory bandwidth of 3.35TB/s. Reading Llama 3.1 8B's 16.06 billion bytes once takes at least 4.8 ms, so one step serves every answer in the batch for about the price of one.

realWorld.title: What a card hour costs
realWorld.text: Lambda's pricing page, read on 16 October 2026, lists the NVIDIA H100 SXM at $4.29 per GPU per hour on a single-card machine (PRICE/GPU/HR). At 730 hours a month that is $3,132; two such cards, $6,263. Prices change; the arithmetic is the lesson.

asked: How would you benchmark a serving engine on your own traffic?
interview.answer: All three take requests, batch them into steps on the GPU and stream tokens back; they differ in how they manage memory, how they batch, and how much is decided before they run. vLLM is the broad default: PagedAttention hands out KV cache in blocks, continuous batching re-forms the batch every step, it sizes the running batch from free GPU memory at run time, and it supports a wide range of models and hardware. SGLang has the same basics and is strongest when prompts share prefixes: RadixAttention keeps shared prefixes' KV cache in a radix tree and reuses it, and its cache-aware router sends requests to the worker most likely to hold their prefix. TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's: in-flight batching and a paged KV cache, often the fastest on NVIDIA GPUs, but in its build flow limits such as max batch size and max num tokens are fixed in the build config, and a TensorRT engine is tied by default to the GPU it was built on. To benchmark on my own traffic I'd record the busiest window from production logs, with arrival times and prompt and output lengths, replay it at the same times into each engine configured exactly as it will run, and compare time to first token and end-to-end latency at the median and the tail, plus throughput and cost per card hour, at the real peak and above it for headroom. I'd check memory for any build-time limit, sweep the limits, and repeat the replay whenever the engine, model, card or traffic changes. A public benchmark tells me which engines are worth replaying, not which one to run: on one night I saw an engine built for 16 at a time win 72 to 55 tokens a second at 12 users and then queue 64 users into four waves, 27.8 seconds for the last answer against 11.1 on vLLM.

terms.def: Replacing a road's worn top layer: planing it off and laying fresh asphalt. Ulceby's crews resurface the motorway past Hatherop at night.
A machine that grinds the worn surface off a road before new asphalt is laid.
The black road surface: stones bound with bitumen, laid hot and rolled flat.
Lanes coned off so crews can work. Ulceby's closures start at 22:00 under permits.
The road authority's written permission to close lanes at set times. It is why every crew starts at 22:00.
A job's written steps and safety rules. Each crew has its own each night, about 1,500 tokens; the assistant sums it up in about 500.
The person who oversees all the night's crews and keeps them in touch by radio. Ebele is Ulceby's.
The person in charge of one crew on site. Ulceby has 64 each night, each with a tablet.
A drain inlet in the road, with a grate, that a planer must avoid.
A program that writes text one small piece at a time, having learned from huge amounts of text (a1e01).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads and writes (a1e03). A summary here is about 500.
The learned numbers a model is made of (a1e02). Llama 3.1 8B's take 16.06 billion bytes in 16 bits, about 15 GB on the card's meter.
Meta's open-weights language model with 8.03 billion weights (a10e01). In 16 bits its file is 16.06 billion bytes; each token's working memory is 128 KB.
Short for graphics card: a board with a GPU, a graphics processing unit, and its own memory (a10e01). Ulceby rents one NVIDIA H100.
A graphics card with 80 GB of memory read at 3.35 TB a second in its SXM version. Ulceby rents one at $4.29 an hour, $3,132 a 730-hour month.
Sizes on the card's meter count 1 GB as 1,024 MB and 1 MB as 1,024 KB; speeds use the maker's 1,000. A TB is a thousand GB.
The program between a model and its users: it loads the model on the card, takes questions, batches them into steps and returns answers. Like a kitchen around one recipe.
A free, widely used serving engine with paged working memory and continuous batching. It decides how many answers run together from free memory as it runs.
NVIDIA's serving engine for its own graphics cards, with in-flight batching and paged memory. In its build flow the limits, such as the largest batch, are fixed when it is built.
A free serving engine that keeps the working memory of prompts' shared beginnings and reuses it (RadixAttention), with a router that sends similar prompts to the same copy.
One pass of writing: the card reads the weights once and every answer in the batch gets one more token (a10e04).
The answers an engine writes side by side, one token each per step, like a cook stirring several pans at once (a10e04).
One answer's place in the batch. The build for 16 has 16; a question with no free slot waits.
The keys and values the model keeps for every token of an answer while writing it, the KV cache (a10e03): 128 KB a token, 250 MB for a 2,000-token question and summary.
Short for key-value cache: the engineers' name for an answer's working memory on the card (a10e03).
Card memory not taken by weights or other answers. vLLM lets in answers while it lasts: 64 need 15.6 GB beside 15 GB of weights on an 80 GB card.
vLLM's way of handing out working memory in small pages as each answer grows, with a table of where they sit (a10e03). Like a notebook given a page at a time.
Re-packing the batch after every step: finished answers leave and waiting ones take the free slots (a10e04). vLLM does it by default.
TensorRT-LLM's name for continuous batching: answers join and leave the batch while it runs, up to the largest batch it was built with.
SGLang's way of keeping the working memory of prompts' opening tokens in a tree, so a new prompt with the same beginning reuses it instead of reading it again.
The opening tokens of a prompt. Questions that start with the same document share a prefix; Ulceby's share only a few words, since each crew's statement is its own.
A second identical engine with the same model on its own card, the questions shared between the copies. Two copies of the build for 16 give 32 slots.
A program in front of several copies that chooses which copy gets each question. SGLang's sends a question to the copy most likely to hold its beginning.
The busiest minute of the night: 22:00, when all 64 crew leaders ask at once as the permits start.
A published speed test: someone else's recorded questions played into engines with their settings. It shows how an engine ran their traffic, not yours.
Recording a stretch of real questions with their arrival times and lengths, playing them into each engine at the same times, and comparing the timings.
Preparing TensorRT-LLM before it runs: choose the model and card, fix the limits, then compile. Changing a fixed limit means building again.
To turn the model and the build's settings into a program for one card.
The most answers an engine runs at once. TensorRT-LLM's docs call it max batch size, set in the build config; the benchmark's recipe set 16, the page's default is 2048.
A limit fixed when an engine is built. With 16: 16 answers run, the rest wait, and a new wave starts as slots free.
TensorRT-LLM's second build-time limit: the most tokens it works on in one step. Its tuning page advises trying it together with the max batch size.
TensorRT-LLM's command for building an engine; --max_batch_size sets the largest batch.
NVIDIA's library that turns a trained model into an engine for its cards. By default its engines are tied to the TensorRT version and the GPU they were built on.
A group of answers that start together when slots free. With 16 slots and 500-token summaries, 64 questions run in four waves of 6.9 s.
How long from asking until the first token arrives (a10e02). The last 16 crews' was 21.0 s on Wednesday night; vLLM's was 0.3 s the week before.
How fast one answer is written. 72 on TensorRT-LLM and 55 on vLLM at 12 at once; 45 on vLLM and 54 on the build for 64 at 64 at once.
The screen of the assistant's timings. Its "answers 30% faster than last week" was typed in at 14:00 from the afternoon test: 72 ÷ 55 = 1.31.
How long the app waits for an answer before giving up. A longer one would not change a 21-second wait.
The international standard for information security management. Annex A 8.6 covers capacity management; 8.32 covers change management.
Making sure systems have the resources the work needs, now and later, by monitoring, testing and planning.
Planning, testing and approving changes to systems before they go live, so a change does what it should on the work it serves.
The international standard for quality management. Clause 8.5.6 covers control of changes.
An audit report on a service's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC8.1 covers authorising, testing and approving changes.

atWork: Look for a serving engine switched on a published benchmark: a faster engine, a newer version or a tuned recipe, tested at daytime load and switched before the busiest hour. It is a common pattern: the benchmark ran someone else's traffic with someone else's settings, and a limit fixed at build time sits above the test and below the peak. Ask four things. When was your engine last measured at your real peak, with your arrival times and lengths? Which of its limits are fixed when it is built, and what are they set to? Does your dashboard show live waits, the first token and the last, or a percentage typed in once? And is a replay run again before every change of engine, model, card or traffic? A later build project will ask you to measure this. Standards-readiness note, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, an auditor checking Annex A 8.6 (capacity management) or 8.32 (change management), as summarised by a third-party guide, would look for a test at the real peak before the switch, with the results recorded. An auditor checking ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.5.6 (control of changes) or SOC 2's CC8.1 (changes to systems) would likely ask the same. How these apply depends on your scope and auditor. This is not legal advice.

recall.prompt: Your team moved its staff chat assistant to a new serving engine after a public benchmark and a daytime test with 10 users at once showed it 40% faster. The engine was built with room for 32 answers in a batch. On Monday at 09:00, when 200 staff log in together, most wait 20 seconds or more for the first word, though the GPU's memory is far from full. What is happening, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The build fixed the largest batch at 32: at 09:00, 32 answers run and the rest wait in waves, whatever room the memory has
The test ran below the limit and the benchmark measured someone else's traffic, so neither met the 09:00 peak
Replay the recorded 09:00 peak (arrival times and lengths) into each engine as built, and rebuild the limit from it with the memory checked

recall.model: The engine was built with a largest batch of 32, a limit fixed at build time. At 09:00, 200 questions arrive together: 32 answers run and the rest wait in waves for free slots, however much memory is free, so most people wait for the first word. The daytime test ran 10 at once, below the limit, and the benchmark measured someone else's traffic with someone else's settings, so neither ever met the 09:00 peak. Record the real peak, with its arrival times and lengths, and replay the recording into each engine exactly as built. Then rebuild the limit from that peak, with headroom, after you check the memory each answer needs, and watch the live wait for the first word, not a percentage from one test.

recall.prompt: An engine built with a largest batch of 16 writes 72 tokens a second for each answer. 64 summaries of 500 tokens are asked for at the same moment. When does the last one finish?
recall.why: Each answer takes 500 ÷ 72 = 6.9 s. Only 16 run at once, so 64 make four waves, starting at 0, 6.9, 13.9 and 20.8 s; the last ends at 4 × 6.94 = 27.8 s. 6.9 s is one wave; 21.0 s is when the last wave's first word arrives; 11.1 s is vLLM running all 64 at once at 45 tokens a second.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: compare vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM, and say how you would benchmark a serving engine on your own traffic.

keyIdeas.idea: vLLM: paged KV cache and continuous batching, batch sized from free memory, broad model and hardware support; SGLang adds reuse of shared prompt beginnings (RadixAttention) with a cache-aware router
TensorRT-LLM: NVIDIA's engine, built for its model and GPU, with limits such as max batch size fixed at build; often fastest below those limits
Record your busiest window with arrival times and lengths, replay it at the same times into each engine as configured, and compare first-token and last-token latency and cost at and above the peak

recall.model: All three batch requests into steps on the GPU and stream tokens back. vLLM uses PagedAttention for its KV cache and continuous batching, sizes the running batch from free memory as it goes, and supports a wide range of models and hardware. SGLang has the same basics and adds RadixAttention, which keeps a shared prefix's KV cache and reuses it, plus a cache-aware router that sends a request to the worker likely to hold its prefix. TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's engine, built for its model and GPU, with in-flight batching and a paged KV cache; limits such as max batch size are fixed in the build config, and below them it is often the fastest. To benchmark on my own traffic I'd record the busiest window from production logs with arrival times and prompt and output lengths, replay it at the same times into each engine as configured for production, and compare time to first token, time to the last token at the median and the tail, throughput and cost, at the peak and above it for headroom.

recall.prompt: Yesterday's test sent 12 questions at once: the new engine wrote 72 tokens a second each, the old one 55, and the dashboard now says 30% faster. What did the test never check?
options: More answers at once than the largest batch
Whether both engines served the same model
How fast the card reads its memory
recall.why: With 12 at once the test stayed under the build's largest batch of 16, so nothing ever waited for a slot. 72 ÷ 55 is 1.31; both engines served Llama 3.1 8B; the card's memory speed is the same whichever engine runs on it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. Since Thursday 8 October the engine has run built for 64, and every 22:00 has answered all 64 crews at once: first word in 0.3 s, every answer in 9.3 s. On Monday 2 November Ulceby won a second contract, the next stretch of the same motorway, and from Monday 7 December its 16 night crews joined ours on the same card and the same 22:00 permits: 80 crew leaders. That night 16 crews waited 9.5 s for their first word, and the last answer finished at 16.2 s. Aurelijus says it's the same engine that passed the replay in October.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did 16 crews wait again, when the engine passed a replay of Ulceby's own peak? What would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The build's limit came from October's peak of 64; 80 crews pass it, so 64 run and 16 wait for a second wave (9.3 s, then their first word at 9.5 s)
A replay is a picture of one peak; run it again whenever the load changes, such as a new contract, and leave headroom
Rebuild with a larger largest batch after a memory check (80 answers: 15 GB + 19.5 GB = 34.5 GB of 80), and alert on questions waiting for a slot

coldCase.model: The engine is the same; the peak changed. The build for 64 was sized from October's peak of 64 crews, and the second contract made it 80, more than 64. So at 22:00, 64 answers run at 54 tokens a second and end at 9.3 s, and the other 16 wait for a second wave: first word at 9.5 s, last answer at 16.2 s. A replay is a picture of one peak, so record the new peak and replay again whenever the load changes, as with a new contract, and leave headroom. Then rebuild the engine with a larger batch after a memory check: 80 answers need 80 × 250 MB = 19.5 GB beside 15 GB of weights, 34.5 GB of 80, and the replay must measure the speed at 80, which nobody has. And alert when any question waits for a slot, so the next growth shows on the dashboard before it shows on the radio.

sources.title: NVIDIA, TensorRT-LLM documentation, Tuning Max Batch Size and Max Num Tokens, read 16 October 2026: One of TensorRT-LLM’s key features is it’s inflight batching scheduler and runtime that handles simultaneously; It cannot schedule the last request, Request 5, even though there is space for it in the max num tokens budget; because of the max batch size limit of 4.; It is important to set the max batch size large enough that it doesn’t bottleneck the scheduling of new requests.; You can specify the max batch size in the build config.; If you are using the CLI flow for building engines pass `--max_batch_size <int>` to `trtllm-build` to tune max batch size.; Sweeping across max batch sizes of 64, 512, and the default 2048 produced the following results; Like Max Batch size, max num tokens is also specified in the build config.; Since max num tokens and max batch size both affect scheduling, grid searching across combinations of them

NVIDIA, TensorRT-LLM documentation, Overview, read 16 October 2026: TensorRT LLM is NVIDIA’s comprehensive open-source library for accelerating and optimizing inference performance; of the latest large language models (LLMs) on NVIDIA GPUs.; In-flight batching eliminates wait times by dynamically managing request execution,; Paged KV cache with intelligent block reuse and memory optimization
NVIDIA, TensorRT documentation 10.x, TensorRT’s Capabilities, read 16 October 2026: By default, TensorRT engines are specific to both the TensorRT version and the GPU on which they were created.

vLLM documentation, home page, read 16 October 2026: vLLM is a fast and easy-to-use library for LLM inference and serving.; Efficient management of attention key and value memory with PagedAttention; Continuous batching of incoming requests, chunked prefill, prefix caching; Support for NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and x86/ARM/PowerPC CPUs.

SGLang documentation, home page (now at docs.sglang.io), read 16 October 2026: High-performance serving framework for large language and multimodal models.; Designed for low-latency, high-throughput inference with RadixAttention, prefix caching, and multi-GPU parallelism.

Lianmin Zheng, Liangsheng Yin, Zhiqiang Xie and others, SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs (arXiv:2312.07104), abstract page, read 16 October 2026: The runtime accelerates execution with novel optimizations like RadixAttention for KV cache reuse; Experiments show that SGLang achieves up to 6.4x higher throughput compared to state-of-the-art inference systems

LMSYS, SGLang v0.4: Zero-Overhead Batch Scheduler, Cache-Aware Load Balancer, Faster Structured Outputs, 4 December 2024, read 16 October 2026: The load balancer predicts prefix KV cache hit rates on workers and selects those with the highest match rates.; Requests are sent to workers with a higher hit rate, and load balancing is performed to avoid imbalance.; up to 1.9x increase in throughput with 3.8x higher cache hit rate
